journey:sadao-watanabe-katazome-christ.l: Impressions in many museum, university and church collections in Japan, the United States and Europe
journey:sadao-watanabe-katazome-christ.m: Hand-coloured stencil prints (katazome) on kozo and momigami paper
journey:sadao-watanabe-katazome-christ.noimg: © Estate of Sadao Watanabe. Impressions can be viewed through museum collections in Japan and the United States.

x.summary: Watanabe retold the Bible in the visual language of Japanese folk art: Christ and the apostles appear with round faces and almond eyes, dressed in kimono and, at the Last Supper, sharing sushi and sake, all framed in bold black lines and earthy reds, ochres and indigos. Using the traditional katazome stencil-dyeing technique, often on crumpled, cloth-like momigami paper, he gave scenes from the Nativity to the Passion a joyful, handmade warmth. His prints became beloved across the world as an image of the Gospel at home in Asian culture.
facts: Watanabe was baptized at seventeen and was deeply influenced by the mingei folk-craft movement of Yanagi Sōetsu and by the master dyer Serizawa Keisuke, from whom he learned the katazome stencil-dyeing technique.
Momigami, the paper he often printed on, is kneaded and crumpled by hand to give it a soft, cloth-like texture; his colours were bound with soybean milk prepared by his wife, Harue.
In 1958 his print The Bronze Serpent won first prize at the Modern Japanese Print Exhibition in New York, and his prints were especially beloved by churches and collectors in the United States.
